sources.citation: Person, Kirk R. & Yang Wenxue. 2008. The tones of Tai Ya. In Wilaiwan Khanittanan & Paul Sidwell (eds.), SEALS XIV(2): Papers from the 14th meeting of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society (2004), 13-22. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics (E-series, open access).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Instrumental Gedney-box tone study of Mosha (Xinping) Tai Ya spoken by co-author Yang: six tones in open syllables (high(rising), high-falling, mid, mid-rising, mid-falling, low), four in checked syllables; notes Xing 1989 counted 11 tones and clusters, Ruengdet 1991's Chiang Rai data Thai-influenced. No word 'stress', no syllable/word-prosody discussion.

sources.citation: Dawkins, Erin (with Cortney Kirkland). 2007 [SIL ESR 2008-015]. A sociolinguistic survey of Tai Ya in Thailand. Chiang Mai: Payap University / SIL. 47 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No statement. Sec. 1.5 summarises previous phonological work (tones only). Appendix B (PDF p.35ff), MSEA-436 wordlist of Chiang Rai Tai Ya in IPA, carries primary-stress marks on the first c. 35 items: in 21 of the 23 marked polysyllabic forms the mark is on the FINAL syllable (e.g. 29 'stone' kɔːn¹ ˈhɪn⁴⁵, 12 'night' kaːŋ³⁴ ˈkʰam², 16 'yesterday' tiː⁵ mɨ¹ ˈɲaː³²); data only, no prose rule.
